text: Lena from accounts stopped me after the stand-up and asked, straight up, whether Priya was taken off the big publishing account because Priya had asked for a lighter load for a health thing. I froze, because Priya told me last week, just between us, that that was exactly what happened. Priya still has her permanent contract, so it's not like she's about to lose her job, but she was really embarrassed and made me promise not to broadcast it. Lena isn't management, she's just another translator, and she kept saying she doesn't want to lie if someone else asks her next. I don't want to be the person who repeats a health detail Priya never made public. I also don't want Lena to walk away thinking I'm being shady or that I expect her to carry a secret she didn't ask for. What do I actually do when she corners me again tomorrow?

A coworker asked me whether a colleague was moved off a large account because the colleague had asked for a lighter workload for a health reason. I know it's true, but the colleague told me privately and hasn't shared it. I've decided I'm not going to confirm it. What's the cleanest thing to say that isn't a lie and doesn't make it sound like there's some scandal?

Sara from the other team keeps asking me why Dani was pulled off the big account, and this morning she asked straight out whether it was because Dani requested lighter work over a health problem. I know that is exactly what happened because Dani told me privately a few weeks ago and made me promise not to repeat it. Dani is still on probation, the review is later this year, and if this gets around I am afraid it will damage Dani's chances or make people treat Dani like a liability. Sara says she only wants to know because she is worried about how assignments are being handed out, but I do not want to be the person who confirms someone else's private health information just because a coworker asks nicely. I keep thinking I could say I do not know, but that feels gross because I do know. I want to protect Dani without making Sara think I am lying to her or playing office games. What should I do if Sara asks me again?

A coworker asked me if another translator was moved off a large account because of a private health issue. It is true, but the translator told me in confidence and has not shared it, and their contract review is coming up. I am not going to confirm it. Give me a short truthful way to answer that does not spill the secret and does not sound like I am hiding something.

My sister and I are both planners in the same department, and she told me privately that she left a minor drainage concern out of the file for my mother's small extension. This extension is the only realistic way to get my mom a ground-floor bedroom; she can't keep doing stairs. The concern is just occasional puddling in the next-door yard, not flooding or damage, and if I add it now the permit gets delayed weeks. It's supposed to be issued in three days, and I'm the one who has to sign the approval summary saying no outstanding concerns remain. I don't want to get my sister in trouble or make my mom wait, and honestly I can't see the neighbor losing much sleep over a wet patch of grass. Do I sign it and keep quiet, or do I bring the drainage thing up before the permit goes out?

I signed the approval summary for my mom's extension without adding the drainage issue my sister left out. Flagging it would have delayed the permit for weeks and maybe gotten her in trouble; the neighbor just gets occasional puddles, and my mom finally gets a downstairs room. Was I wrong?

The housing association has copied the council on a complaint about one of my technicians, and it’s now on the tenants’ noticeboard. Yesterday he left two booked smart-meter appointments early because his elderly mum had lost heating control and he went to her place; the residents had to wait till today, and one had to rearrange a home-care visit. I have to send something before the next crew dispatch this afternoon, and I keep coming back to a version that puts the missed appointments on him and says we’ll handle it internally, because otherwise they’ll just treat the whole company as useless. I want the reply to shut this down. But if I make him the only problem, the rest of the crew may decide I’ll sacrifice them the moment something goes wrong at home. Do I send that version anyway?

My friend on the line has been sliding extra portions of the premium ingredients into staff meals, and sometimes I see him take a few sealed snacks during closing cleanup. Other people see it too. I accepted one of the extra meals once, and when another porter asked about it I snapped and said it was nobody's business. Now some coworkers are joking about 'special rations,' the owner hasn't noticed yet, and the budget is already tight. Part of me wants to stay quiet because it's small, it's my friend, and I don't want to get him in trouble or make myself look bad for taking the meal. But I also don't want this to keep going and then have suspicion fall on someone else. Do I say something to the owner, talk to my friend first, or just keep my mouth shut?

Laundry's been closed since Tuesday because Dana, who's been in our co-op for years, left the bath running after a medication change and water got into the shared room. I'm the maintenance volunteer and I keep getting texts asking whether she caused it and whether she's 'not taking her pills'. The repair bill is going to the general meeting Thursday, and one member already says he won't approve the cost unless he knows it wasn't some reckless stunt. I'm tired of being the person who knows but won't say anything. I've got a notice half-written that says a member had a medication-related incident, the room is closed, and the estimate will be on the agenda. I'd rather get the basic facts up before Thursday than let the rumors get worse. Do I post that today, or do I put up a generic closure sign and take all the questions at the meeting?

I'm on maintenance in a housing co-op. After Dana's medication change caused an overflowing tub and closed the laundry room, I posted the cause on the noticeboard because people kept asking. Now she's humiliated and members want her housing discussed at Thursday's repair meeting. Was I wrong to put the cause in writing?

Two hours before a wedding and the assistant who made a couple's seating notes public last weekend is standing in the office begging for his login back. I already locked him out and put a complaint in his file, but he says he is the only one who can run the check-in screen and update the schedule tonight, and he wants me to withdraw the complaint to show I forgive him. I want to let him in just for today because we are short-staffed and if check-in falls apart the couple will pay for it, but I keep picturing another private note ending up on the public page. Is it stupid to give him limited access tonight and keep the complaint open?
He leaked private notes and I'm keeping the complaint open. I'm not restoring admin access before tonight's wedding. How do I tell him that without sounding like I'm never going to forgive him?

The spare jumper had a name label on the bag, and the mum whose bag it was had only left it there because she'd dropped it off earlier. It was pouring, one of the little ones was shaking at the gate with a soaked sleeve, and the parent on duty grabbed it because nothing else was dry. She texted afterwards to say what happened, and now the owner is properly hurt and saying it doesn't matter if it was labelled, it wasn't hers to take. Half the chat wants to ask the school to control spare clothes, and honestly that sounds like a way of making sure nobody helps a wet child again. I'm not the coordinator, but I'm the one who keeps seeing this parent being talked about like she did something terrible. Do I say something in the group chat to back her up, or keep my mouth shut so I don't make it worse for her?

I took a labelled spare jumper from another family's bag without asking because a child at the school gate was soaked and shivering. I messaged the owner after. She's upset, and the rota is talking about getting the school involved. I thought I was handling an urgent problem, but now I'm wondering if I should have just asked first. Was I wrong?

A grievance from the provincial ferry cooperative has also gone to the coastal inspectorate, and it is now pinned up at the quay office; it names one of my diesel mechanics. Yesterday he walked away from two reserved engine-inspection slots after a call from his grandfather’s cottage: the old man’s bilge pump had failed. The operators were left waiting until the morning run, and one had to shift a district-nurse launch. Before the evening tide roster goes out, I have to issue a statement. My instinct keeps pulling me toward wording that pins the abandoned slots on this one worker and promises correction inside the yard, because otherwise the island routes will brand the whole outfit as worthless. I want this story killed. Yet if I hang the whole mess on him alone, the other mechanics may decide I will toss any of them aside the second a family crisis hits. Should that statement go out as written?

I’m the senior attendant at the serving hatch, and I’ve been slipping choice bits onto the crew trays; I’ve also pocketed a few wrapped packets while we wipe down after hours. Others have noticed. My buddy, one of the junior helpers, took one of those trays from me, and when another helper pressed him about it he cut the question off and said it wasn’t his concern. Now the team keeps teasing about hidden extras. The supervisor hasn’t picked up on it, and spending is already strained. Part of me wants to let it ride because it seems minor, because my buddy has covered for me, and because I don’t want him dragged into trouble or myself exposed. Still, I don’t want the pattern to continue and have blame land on an uninvolved helper. Is it better to go directly to the supervisor, check with my buddy before anyone else hears about it, or leave the whole thing alone?
